sections.h2: Why is selling a house in New York City different from selling elsewhere?
sections.html:
The city is five boroughs and five counties, so the recording office and paperwork depend on where the house stands. Manhattan is New York County, Brooklyn is Kings County, Queens and the Bronx share names with their counties, and Staten Island is Richmond County.

The Department of Finance sorts every property into one of four tax classes by use. A house of up to three units falls in Class 1, and co-ops and most condominiums go in Class 2. The city also runs its own transfer tax. This page concentrates on houses rather than co-op shares.

For July 1, 2025 the Census Bureau estimates 8,584,629 residents, down 2.5 percent from the 2020 base, packed at 29,303 people per square mile over about 300 square miles of land.

sections.h2: How do the boroughs differ for someone with a house to sell?
sections.html:
Staten Island is the most suburban and calls itself the Borough of Parks, with about 12,300 acres of protected parkland. The Bronx is the only borough on the mainland and holds Pelham Bay Park, the city's largest at 2,772 acres. Queens is the biggest by area and has JFK and LaGuardia airports within its lines.

Brooklyn has the most residents and a long beachfront that includes Coney Island. Manhattan is the smallest and densest borough, at more than 70,000 people per square mile.

  • Staten Island: Richmond County, tied to Brooklyn by the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge and to Manhattan by a free ferry
  • The Bronx: home to Co-op City, the largest cooperatively owned housing complex in the country
  • Queens: on Long Island, north and east of Brooklyn
  • Brooklyn: at the western tip of Long Island

sections.h2: How many New Yorkers own their homes?
sections.html:
Fewer than a third do. The 2020 to 2024 Census figures show owners in 32.8 percent of households, a typical owned-home value of $777,600 and a typical rent of $1,821.

That leaves a renter-heavy city where houses are a modest slice. The city has 3,334,088 households of about 2.48 people each, with a median household income of $80,483 in 2024 dollars. Foreign-born residents are 36.6 percent of the population, and 47.7 percent of people over four speak another language at home.

Workers spend 40.3 minutes getting to their jobs, the longest figure among the four places in this Census comparison. If your house sits near a subway stop or commuter rail line, lead the listing with that.

sections.h2: How is property tax calculated and billed on a New York City house?
sections.html:
The tax year runs from July 1 to June 30, and each property is billed by tax class and assessed value. A property assessed at $250,000 or less is billed four times a year, and one above that is billed twice.

Tax classWhat it coversRate for tax year 2026
Class 1Most residential property of up to three units19.843%
Class 2Other primarily residential property, such as co-ops and condos12.439%
Class 3Property with gas, telephone or electric company equipment11.108%
Class 4All other property, such as offices and warehouses10.848%

Source: NYC Department of Finance property tax rates and glossary pages.

Quarterly bills come due on the first of July, October, January and April, each with a grace period to the 15th. Twice-a-year bills fall on July 1 and January 1. Settling the whole year by the July due date earns a 0.50 percent discount, and interest on late balances compounds daily. If a bill is still open when you sell, ask your closing attorney how it will be handled at closing.

sections.h2: When must a house owner contest an assessment in New York City?
sections.html:
The NYC Tax Commission, an independent agency, takes the appeal, and a Class 1 owner must file by March 15. Classes 2, 3 and 4 face March 1, and late filings are denied. The Commission can lower an assessment, change the tax class and adjust exemptions.

Finance has a separate track: a Request for Review to correct a description or clerical slip, due March 15 for Class 1 and April 1 for other classes. It does not replace an appeal, so file both when both apply.

Owners of high-value homes that are not their primary residence face a newer charge. A law effective May 28, 2026 adds a surcharge of 0.8 percent of market value on one, two and three-family houses worth $5 million or more, climbing to 1.05 and 1.3 percent at higher values. A house used as a primary residence by the owner, a tenant or a relative is exempt. The 2026-27 exemption deadline was October 13, 2026, and any charge shows on the bill due January 1, 2027.

sections.h2: What comes out of the sale price at a New York City closing?
sections.html:
Several layers apply. The seller owes the state's base tax of $2 per $500 of price, and the city adds its own real property transfer tax, normally settled with the other closing costs. For residential conveyances at $3 million or more, the state tacks on a further $1.25 per $500, also on the seller.

The buyer's side has the mansion tax at 1 percent from $1 million up, plus a supplemental tax between 0.25 and 2.9 percent once a residential price reaches $2 million. The city return, Form NYC-RPT, is created online in ACRIS, the Automated City Register Information System. Both parties sign it, and a late return adds 5 percent of the tax per month, capped at 25 percent.

Your attorney can quote the exact city figure, which varies with the kind of transfer and the price. A seller living outside New York State must work out the gain and pay any estimated income tax unless an exemption on Form TP-584-NYC applies.

sections.h2: What does a certificate of occupancy have to do with a New York City sale?
sections.html:
The certificate states the legal use of a building, and nobody may lawfully occupy a structure until the Department of Buildings issues either a final certificate or a temporary one (TCO). A final certificate never expires, but the Department will not issue one while the property has open applications or open violations.

To obtain a final certificate, the Department requires:

  • Final construction, plumbing, elevator and electrical inspection sign-offs
  • A final building survey and an Owner's Cost Affidavit
  • No open applications and no open violations

Buildings put up before 1938 may not need one. A Letter of No Objection from the borough office can document their legal use. Search your address in DOB NOW to see whether a certificate is on file.

The Department urges buyers to close on a final certificate, since an expired and unrenewed TCO can make a house hard to insure, sell or refinance. If you finished a basement or built an extension without closing out the job, a cash buyer taking the house as-is will price that in, so resolve or disclose it before accepting an offer.

faqs.q: On what dates do New York City property tax bills come due?
faqs.a: July 1 and January 1 for twice-a-year payers. Quarterly payers also owe on October 1 and April 1, with a grace period running to the 15th.

faqs.q: What is the 2026 tax rate for a one-family house in the city?
faqs.a: The Department of Finance sets the Class 1 rate at 19.843 percent. Class 1 covers most residential property of up to three units, so a one-family house falls in it.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my house assessment?
faqs.a: Until March 15 for Class 1, filed with the NYC Tax Commission. Owners of Class 2, 3 and 4 property must file by March 1.

faqs.q: Who bears the state transfer tax in a city sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays the base $2 per $500 unless the contract says otherwise. The buyer pays the mansion tax when the price is $1 million or more.

faqs.q: Is a certificate of occupancy required to sell?
faqs.a: Not always. A house built before 1938 may lack one, and a Letter of No Objection from the Department of Buildings can show its legal use. For anything newer or altered, expect the buyer's attorney to ask.
